Subject: Flexible Annual Commit Architectures — Hosted API pricing & SLA credits

Hi Sam,

Thanks again for the time today — enjoyed hearing more about Acme's roadmap for embedding search and personalization across your storefront. Per our conversation, attaching a short note on a flexible annual commit architecture that balances predictable unit economics with burst capacity and SLA crediting. High level: 

- Starter / Growth / Enterprise commit bands (250k / 2M / 10M tokens annually) with step-down per-token pricing and month-by-month carryover for unused committed tokens.
- Graceful overage: small buffer at +15% at committed rates, then metered overage at a mid-tier rate; large bursts routed to on-demand pool to preserve latency.
- SLA crediting: credit tiers tied to 99.9% and 99.5% p99 latency at the committed capacity; credits apply to monthly invoice rather than changing discounts.

I'd like to propose we put together a short spreadsheet with three example profiles (Acme P0 pilot, Q3 ramp, and steady-state enterprise) to show unit economics and billing flow. Looping in Laura to drive commercial terms and next steps.

Next steps: I'll share the example spreadsheet by EOD Friday and propose a brief sync next week to align procurement and SRE expectations.

Best,
Vanessa Ortiz
Director, Strategic Accounts
Redwood Inference

On Thu, Apr 21, 2027 at 10:03 AM Sam Cho <sam.cho@acme.com> wrote:
> Vanessa,

> Appreciate the recap. A few clarifying Qs from procurement and infra:

> 1) For the Starter band, what does carryover mean practically? Can unused tokens in Q1 be applied in Q4?

Great questions — short answers first, detail below.

1) Carryover policy: unused committed tokens roll forward quarter-to-quarter within the same contract year but expire at year-end unless you purchase an extension. So Q1 unused can be used in Q2/Q3/Q4 but not post-contract unless we agree on carry-forward credits in the renewal. This keeps accounting simple for both sides.

2) Sustained burst handling: for sustained bursts we use a tiered approach — short bursts (<72h) are absorbed out of the platform burst buffer at committed rates; medium bursts (72h–14d) billed at a pre-agreed surge rate (about 40% above committed per-token) unless you opt into temporary dedicated capacity; long sustained surges (>14d) trigger a playbook with your account team to provision Dedicated or increase the commit band. Throttling is a last resort and would be communicated in advance with traffic shaping options.

3) SLA credits: we can surface credits on the same invoice month as either a line-item credit against committed spend or as a credit note depending on your accounting preference. We'll ask finance to confirm the exact flow, but procurement's preference to apply credits within the same invoice month is acceptable in principle.

I'll hand the spreadsheet to Rishi (SE) to show modeled scenarios and to Laura to respond on MSA: Laura — can you run the MSA/SLAs against Redwood's commercial templates and procurement's preferred flow?

Thanks,
Vanessa

Hi Sam / Vanessa,

I've attached a simple workbook with three modeled customer profiles and the math behind the proposed surges, carryover, and the SLA crediting mechanisms. Key tabs:

- SUMMARY: headline unit economics for Starter/Growth/Enterprise (tokens, committed price, effective blended price with typical carryover profiles)
- SCENARIOS: month-by-month run-rate for a pilot -> ramp -> steady state customer, showing where carryover helps and when surge rates are triggered
- SLA_CREDITS: worked examples showing how credits flow into month-end invoices for p99 or availability misses

Highlights from the models: 
- Example: Growth band (2M tokens): committed price $0.0009/token, effective price drops to $0.00075/token if 15% carryover used optimally across Q2–Q4.
- Burst handling: 72h buffer covers ~95th percentile traffic from client telemetry; beyond that the surge rate keeps the cost predictable while we spin up Dedicated capacity if it looks sustained.
- SLA credits: modeled as invoice line-item credits; if you prefer a cash refund we can do that for enterprise deals but it requires finance sign-off.
